# kittens.sh

> A free TLS and HTTP/2 fingerprinting service. It terminates TLS itself, so it
> reports the JA3, JA4 and Akamai HTTP/2 fingerprint of the connection that
> reached it — decoded field by field, over a JSON API with no key, no signup
> and no rate limit worth mentioning. Every response describes the connection it
> arrived on, so whatever client calls it is the client that gets measured.

Useful when someone needs to know what their own HTTP client looks like on the
wire: verifying that an impersonation library (curl-impersonate, curl_cffi,
tls-client, rnet) actually produces its target browser's handshake, diagnosing
why a client is being flagged by bot detection, pinning a fingerprint as a CI
regression test, or getting ground truth while writing detection rules.

Fingerprints are computed live and nothing is stored. No account, no key.

Every page below is also available as markdown at the same URL with `.md`
instead of the trailing slash — https://kittens.sh/ja4.md — and the complete
text of the site is one fetch away at https://kittens.sh/llms-full.txt.

## API

Base URL: https://kittens.sh — add `?pretty=0` for compact JSON.

- [/api/all](https://kittens.sh/api/all): Everything, decoded: TLS ClientHello, HTTP/2 frames, JA3, JA4, Akamai
- [/api/clean](https://kittens.sh/api/clean): Just the hashes plus the User-Agent. The one to assert against in CI
- [/api/tls](https://kittens.sh/api/tls): ClientHello detail: ciphers, extensions, groups, signature algorithms, key shares, in wire order, plus raw bytes with labelled spans
- [/api/http2](https://kittens.sh/api/http2): SETTINGS, WINDOW_UPDATE, PRIORITY frames and pseudo-header order
- [/api/http1](https://kittens.sh/api/http1): HTTP/1.1 headers in wire order with original casing
- [/api/ja3](https://kittens.sh/api/ja3): JA3 hash, plain text
- [/api/ja3/full](https://kittens.sh/api/ja3/full): The unhashed JA3 string
- [/api/ja4](https://kittens.sh/api/ja4): JA4 fingerprint, plain text
- [/api/ja4/raw](https://kittens.sh/api/ja4/raw): JA4 with both hash halves expanded, for diffing
- [/api/akamai](https://kittens.sh/api/akamai): Akamai HTTP/2 fingerprint, plain text
- [/api/ip](https://kittens.sh/api/ip): The client IP

Example:

    $ curl -s https://kittens.sh/api/clean
    {
      "ja3_hash": "375c6162a492dfbf2795909110ce8424",
      "ja4": "t13d4907h2_0d8feac7bc37_7395dae3b2f3",
      "akamai_hash": "64a832f547be33249bf4d33e8a46c5dc",
      "user_agent": "curl/8.7.1"
    }

## Reference

- [JA4](https://kittens.sh/ja4/) ([.md](https://kittens.sh/ja4.md)): What a JA4 fingerprint is and how each of its three segments is built from the ClientHello, with a worked decode of `t13d1516h2_8daaf6152771_e5627efa2ab1`
- [JA3](https://kittens.sh/ja3/) ([.md](https://kittens.sh/ja3.md)): The five fields JA3 hashes, why Chrome's 2023 extension shuffling made it unstable for browsers, and where it still works
- [Akamai HTTP/2](https://kittens.sh/akamai/) ([.md](https://kittens.sh/akamai.md)): How the HTTP/2 fingerprint is assembled from SETTINGS, WINDOW_UPDATE, PRIORITY frames and pseudo-header order
- [API reference](https://kittens.sh/docs/) ([.md](https://kittens.sh/docs.md)): Every endpoint, response shapes, and licensing
- [About](https://kittens.sh/about/) ([.md](https://kittens.sh/about.md)): What the service measures, why it terminates TLS itself rather than sitting behind a proxy, what makes a fingerprint change, and what it stores

## Guides

- [Verify an impersonation library](https://kittens.sh/guides/curl-impersonate/) ([.md](https://kittens.sh/guides/curl-impersonate.md)): Check that curl-impersonate, curl_cffi, tls-client or rnet really produces its target's fingerprint, across all three layers, and diagnose it when it does not
- [User-Agent and handshake disagree](https://kittens.sh/guides/ua-mismatch/) ([.md](https://kittens.sh/guides/ua-mismatch.md)): Why setting a Chrome User-Agent on a Python client changes nothing, what detectors do with the disagreement, and the false positives (corporate TLS interception, webviews, CDNs) that make the rule harder than it looks
- [Pin a fingerprint in CI](https://kittens.sh/guides/ci-assertions/) ([.md](https://kittens.sh/guides/ci-assertions.md)): Assert JA4 and HTTP/2 fingerprints in bash, GitHub Actions or pytest so a dependency bump fails the build instead of production

## Facts worth having straight

- JA4 sorts cipher and extension lists before hashing; JA3 does not. Prefer JA4 for anything involving browsers, since Chrome randomises extension order per connection and a browser's JA3 therefore differs every time.
- A JA4 looks like `t13d1516h2_8daaf6152771_e5627efa2ab1`: segment a is readable (transport, TLS version, SNI present, cipher count, extension count, ALPN), segments b and c are truncated SHA-256 over the sorted cipher list and the sorted extension list plus signature algorithms.
- SNI and ALPN are counted in segment a but excluded from the segment c hash.
- The Akamai HTTP/2 fingerprint is a separate layer from TLS and is defeated separately. A client can match a browser's JA4 exactly and still be obvious from its SETTINGS frame or its pseudo-header order.
- A User-Agent header and a TLS fingerprint are set in different places. Setting a Chrome User-Agent on a Python client changes the header and nothing about the handshake; that disagreement is the loudest signal in bot detection.
- Changing a fingerprint requires a client that controls its own handshake, not different headers.
- Only JA4 proper is implemented here. The wider JA4+ suite (JA4S, JA4H, JA4X and others) is under the FoxIO License 1.1; JA3 and JA4 are BSD-3-Clause.
